title: "A corpus proportion"
execute:
  enabled: true

The IID model on the [independent-sampling page](independent-sampling.qmd#identical-distributions-and-independence) used the actual accusative labels in UD Turkish BOUN. We now connect that coding to the mean and variance of a Bernoulli variable.

We will start with the source `Case` annotation and define a binary random variable from it. The sample mean of the realized indicators gives the pooled accusative proportion; under the Bernoulli model, the random variable has mean $p$ and variance $p(1-p)$. We will then break the pooled summary apart by register to see which variation it has averaged over.

Recall that a [random variable](../random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables.qmd) maps each possible outcome to a number. Its [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) is the expected squared deviation from its expectation. Here the numerical map is the zero--one case recoding, while randomness enters only through the working sampling model.

## From annotation to random variable

One row remains one personal-pronoun token nested in a sampled sentence. The binary response is a deterministic recoding of the source UD `Case` value:

$$
X_i=\mathbb I\{\text{case}_i=\text{Acc}\}.
$$

For instance, a row whose source label is `Case=Acc` is recoded as one; a row labeled `Case=Abl` is recoded as zero. Nothing random happens during this recoding. Randomness enters only when we posit a sampling model for which token rows might have been observed.

```{r}
#| label: load-ud-corpus-proportion
library(ggplot2)

pronouns <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/personal-pronoun-cases.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
pronouns$accusative_check <- as.integer(pronouns$case == "Acc")

stopifnot(identical(pronouns$accusative, pronouns$accusative_check))

n <- nrow(pronouns)
k <- sum(pronouns$accusative)
p_hat <- mean(pronouns$accusative)
bernoulli_variance <- p_hat * (1 - p_hat)

data.frame(
  tokens = n,
  accusative_tokens = k,
  observed_proportion = p_hat,
  fitted_bernoulli_variance = bernoulli_variance
)
```

```{r}
#| label: show-ud-indicator-rows
pronouns[c(1L, which(pronouns$accusative == 1L)[1L]),
  c("sentence_text", "form", "case", "accusative")]
```

For $X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$, the two possible values give

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]
=0(1-p)+1(p)=p
$$

and, because $X^2=X$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}[X]
&=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2\\
&=p-p^2\\
&=p(1-p).
\end{aligned}
$$

The sample analogue of the mean is

$$
\widehat p=\overline X
=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i
=\frac{k}{n}.
$$

For this release, the visible code yields $\widehat p=$ `r sprintf("%.4f", p_hat)` and the fitted Bernoulli variance `r sprintf("%.4f", bernoulli_variance)`.

This fitted model variance is $\widehat p(1-\widehat p)$. The ordinary unbiased sample variance of the zero-one rows is instead $s^2=n\widehat p(1-\widehat p)/(n-1)$. The two are close for large $n$, but they answer different questions: the first plugs the estimated Bernoulli parameter into a model formula, while the second estimates row variance with a finite-sample correction.

## Variation hidden by the pooled proportion

```{r}
#| label: plot-ud-corpus-proportion
register_summary <- aggregate(
  accusative ~ register,
  data = pronouns,
  FUN = function(x) c(tokens = length(x), proportion = mean(x))
)
register_plot <- data.frame(
  register = register_summary$register,
  tokens = register_summary$accusative[, "tokens"],
  proportion = register_summary$accusative[, "proportion"]
)

ggplot(register_plot, aes(register, proportion)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = p_hat, color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(size = tokens), color = "grey25") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1)) + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  labs(x = "BOUN register", y = "Accusative proportion", size = "Tokens") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The pooled proportion describes the release under this coding. It does not explain case choice, and the register differences suggest that one shared probability may be too restrictive. Case depends on grammatical function and construction, while token rows also inherit sentence-level dependence.

## Recap and forward link

1. The indicator is a deterministic recoding of annotation; the Bernoulli model supplies randomness.
2. A zero-one sample mean is a sample proportion.
3. Fitted Bernoulli variance and unbiased sample variance differ by the $n/(n-1)$ correction.
4. Pooling hides register and syntactic structure.

The [maximum likelihood page](maximum-likelihood.qmd#probability-and-likelihood) asks which shared probability makes the observed labels most probable under this working model.

## Check your understanding

1. Why does the mean of the indicator equal a proportion?
2. Derive the Bernoulli variance using $\mathbb{E}[X^2]$.
3. What does the red line represent in the figure?
4. Name a syntactic predictor that a substantive model of Turkish case might include.

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The indicator is one for an accusative token and zero otherwise, so its sample mean is the number of accusative tokens divided by the number of tokens. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. $\mathbb{E}[X^2]=\mathbb{E}[X]=p$ because $X^2=X$. Thus $\operatorname{Var}[X]=p-p^2=p(1-p)$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The red line is the pooled accusative proportion across all qualifying BOUN release rows. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. A substantive model might include grammatical function, such as whether the pronoun is a direct object. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
